summary:
Day 4 of #12daysofCodexStratfin on how we use Codex on OpenAI's finance team.
Scott Dean uses Codex to create a custom finance dashboards from scratch for the Robotics team: P&L highlights, actuals vs. forecast comparisons, variance callouts, trend views, headcount detail, and data notes. He uses the dashboard in executive business reviews to explain month-over-month changes, highlight the key drivers, and give our Robotics team a simple way to self-serve insights without digging through spreadsheets.
Before Codex 🙁 Building a custom finance dashboard used to mean translating business questions into specs, finding BI or engineering support, waiting for prioritization, and repeating the cycle for every tweak. Even simple changes to layout, commentary, or data views could take longer than the analysis itself. For a finance user without coding experience, creating a polished, shareable web dashboard was possible, but not realistically self-service.
Agentic dawn! 🙂 With Codex, the workflow changes completely. Codex became a thought partner: Who is the audience? What decisions should the dashboard support? What metrics, tables, commentary, and visuals matter most? Once the plan is clear, Codex writes the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, helps iterate on the design, and can support a repeatable refresh workflow. The dashboard can be updated with new data, validated, and republished to an internal page.
The big unlock: finance teams can build tailored tools directly, without waiting on a traditional software development cycle.

Codex enables the team to drill from the cost-center level into the underlying purchase orders, transactions, and accruals to understand what changed and trace each variance back to its source.

summary:
Day 8 of #12daysofChatCodexStratfin on how OpenAI's finance team uses Codex.
Stacy Young uses Codex to reinvent how we forecast and operate OpenAI's Ads business.
Before Codex 🙁 Ads is one of our newest—and spikiest—businesses. Demand shifts with user behavior, weekdays, holidays, and seasonality. We maintained separate monthly and weekly forecast models, then spent countless hours reconciling them every time assumptions changed.
Agentic dawn 🙂 We taught Codex how our Ads business works. Now it automatically translates our monthly plan into weekly and daily operating forecasts, with richer weekday and holiday logic than our old models. The bigger unlock was the app the team built around it. Every historical and current forecast now lives in one interactive Python application where we can:
• Compare forecast versions
• Toggle across daily, weekly, and monthly views
• Slice metrics by any dimension
• Track actuals against plan
No coding background required. Instead of fighting spreadsheet complexity, Stacy now spends her time asking better questions and exploring the business from more angles.

it’s 10pm, june 21st. the summer solstice. you stumble out of a tiny west village wine bar where you had three glasses of orange wine. the waiter kept saying “skin contact” - “how sexy” you thought. sold.
you just spent 2 hours catching up with a high school friend you haven’t seen in ages because for some reason you’re never in the same city at the same time. you laughed about all the ridiculous things you did as kids and gawked at the first wave of your former classmates who are starting to get engaged. you can’t believe you’ve hit that age.
as you’re orienting yourself for the walk home, you search for the usual landmarks. “world trade center is south…i need to go east…hmmm turning around…”
first you catch it in the corner of your eye. then you do a double take. “there’s no way….” you think to yourself. you take a few steps back and look up at the giant glowing billboard displaying an image of a clustered god-knows-what room. it’s a codex ad.
at first you’re confused. what is it doing here? the only people around are tipsy 20-something-corporate-worker-former-greek-life-members and food delivery drivers. it feels like seeing your nerdiest friend at a frat party.
you look again and it starts to settle in that this billboard does not look so out of place. it’s reminiscent of any of the warmly lit windows on the 2nd floor of the surrounding west village townhouses. the scenes are not much different from the bedroom of your best friend.
“god damn it they fucking got me” you think to yourself. you snap a pic, you turn around once more, you find east, and you walk home. on the walk home the only thing you can think is “i can’t wait to go back and pump out some more bullshit.”

That's how he closed a $18M round.

Bolt and Lovable tried to crack mobile. They couldn't. Because they'd never shipped mobile apps. Daniel and his co-founder @Levan have spent their entire careers doing exactly that and it shows.

Day 11 of #12daysofChatCodexStratfin where we show how OpenAI's finance team is using our own technology.
Guilherme Souza uses ChatGPT for Excel and Google Sheets to bring the agentic approach into the spreadsheet, which is becoming an AI-native interface.
What used to take finance teams days - building a multi-product, multi-scenario long-range planning model - can now happen in hours.
The interesting part isn't writing formulas faster. It's being able to say:
"Add a new product."
"Model a recession scenario."
"Flow the changes through revenue, COGS, OPEX, cash flow, and reporting."
...and have the workbook update coherently.
Finance still owns the assumptions and judgment.
AI increasingly owns the spreadsheet plumbing. Less spreadsheet engineering. More financial thinking.

summary:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL91ztrXoAAnLJ_.png
Quoting @bcherny
As engineering, product, design, DS, etc. melt into a new kind of role, I was reflecting on what roles might look like in the future. For example, when I look at the Claude Code team I see what I think is five archetypes:
1. Prototyper: comes up with brand new ideas; churns out many ideas, most of which don't ship
2. Builder: quickly turns a prototype/idea into production-grade product/infra
3. Sweeper: cleans up the UI, simplifies the code and system, unships, optimizes performance
4. Grower: takes a product that has been built and iterates on it to improve Product-Market Fit
5. Maintainer: owns a mature system to make it secure, reliable, fast, and efficient as it scales
Many people span across 2 roles, and sometimes 3 roles. I also notice that these roles are not really tied to job function -- eg. across Anthropic, some designers match category 1, some 2, some 3; same for engineers, PM, DS.
A healthy team needs a mix of these, depending on the product:
- A product that is new and pre-PMF needs people that are strong at 1+2+3
- A product that is growing and has found PMF needs 2+3+4 and some 5
- A product that has strong PMF needs 3+4+5 and some 2
Maybe product roles of the future will look more like this, and less like the domain-specific roles of today?

clean_title: Advice to young engineers: rest is part of the work
summary:
advice to young engineers:
brother, I know you got that dog in you,
but you have to rest too.
In a world where you can do 10,000 things at the same time, you have to remember that rest is part of the work.
If you find yourself at 3:00 p.m on Thursday afternoon and you realize you've done all your work, take a breather. Go outside, stretch your arms out, and feel the sun on your face.
There will be some day in the future where you're going to have to work until 4:00am in the morning.
There will be some some day in the future where you know you need to push through the weekend.
But if you find yourself having a moment to breathe, just breathe.
We do not exist in a world that tells you that you cannot do anything anymore.
We only exist in a world where you are telling yourself to keep going.
You have to think of yourself as some kind of high-performance athlete.
You have to give yourself someone who, when they rolled their ankle in the third quarter, can push through.
We have to realize that those people have offseasons.
We have to realize those people invest in recovery.
But we live in a world where psychological capital feels more infinite than just the limitations of a biological body.
And you have to listen to your body.
clean_summary:
Advice to young engineers: you have to rest too. In a world where you can do many things at once, remember that taking breaks is essential. If you finish your work early in the day, take a moment to breathe, go outside, and feel the sun. There will be times in the future when you'll need to work late or push through the weekend, but when you have a chance to pause, just breathe.

We live in a world that encourages constant effort, but it's important to listen to your body and prioritize recovery. Like high-performance athletes, you need to invest in rest and recovery, recognizing that even the best need offseasons. Psychological resilience is finite, and respecting your biological limits is key to sustainable success.

title: jason (@jxnlco)
clean_title: Taste as a skill of modeling what people will like and taking risks
summary:
transcribed notes on taste:
If you want taste, you're gonna have to eat.
I think now, as AI has allowed more and more people to create things, the biggest differentiation, the biggest skill people are lacking, is taste itself.
What does that mean, right? Taste is a little bit of aesthetic judgment, knowing what's beautiful. But I think taste is really your ability to model out what people will like. And a lot of that requires you to not just consume, right? Like if you want to be a good chef, you have to eat at people's restaurants. You can't just look at the menu.
It's curation versus consumption. And with AI there's so much more volume of work now, so it's really easy to regress to the mean. In which case it's not really taste. Taste is a kind of risk-taking. You're choosing to deviate from the safe average.
There's this story about Kobori Enshū, the tea master who came after Rikyū. A student told him, your taste must be even better than Rikyū's, because everything you collect, everyone agrees is beautiful. Rikyū's collection, only Rikyū could appreciate. And Enshū said no, that's exactly why I'm the lesser man. I was just picking what most people would like. Rikyū had the courage to love things only he could see.
I felt this in art school. My taste exceeded my ability. I could see what good work looked like, I just couldn't make it yet, and I didn't have the words to describe what was going on. Now AI flips that. Ability is basically free, so for most people, ability exceeds taste. You can make anything, and you don't know what's worth making.
Walter Benjamin talked about mechanical reproduction stripping the aura from art. I think AI does something worse. It gives you the destination without the hours of noticing that used to get you there.
In music, transcribing a solo forces you to listen deeply, right? You sit there rewinding the same four bars over and over. AI can just give you the chart. But it gives you the chart, not the ear. So AI doesn't just strip the aura from art, it strips the aura from learning.
The felt distance that made a skill feel earned.
This has been true for how I learned pottery, right? I can't mechanistically learn pottery. I just have to feel and listen to my intuition.
You know, there are video games that don't allow minimaps, because the designers felt that by having waypoints, players would just walk from one area to another and not really notice where anything is. And we don't really wander down streets anymore. We take Ubers that take us there directly. We used to learn places by wandering. Now we follow the blue line.
So if AI shifts the bottleneck from making to noticing, then apprenticeship has to be reinvented around attention.
Taste grows with attention. If the tools remove the attention, you have to put it back.
clean_summary: Taste involves aesthetic judgment and the ability to model what others will enjoy, which requires active curation rather than passive consumption. With AI increasing work volume, there's a tendency to regress to the mean, but true taste involves risk-taking and deviating from the safe average. The story of tea master Kobori Enshū illustrates that loving things only he could see demonstrates greater courage than simply collecting what everyone finds beautiful. AI shifts the skill bottleneck from making to noticing, risking the loss of attention that makes skills feel earned. To preserve taste and learning, attention must be reinvested in the process, as tools that remove attention demand a reinvention of apprenticeship around awareness.

clean_title: The pursuit of speed and excellence without needing justification
summary:
Mind boggling to me that I can make a thing faster and there's always people that ask "but why?" What kind of mentality is that? The pursuit of excellence does not need justification. Also, I find in so many cases, we can't know the impact of an improvement until we do it.
For example, one I've talked about before: Ghostty's high IO throughput has enabled terminal program (emulator and TUI) fuzzing at a speed thats incomparably fast to prior solutions. This has resulted in upstream patches to resolve issues in popular projects like btop, tmux, and more.
Speed enabled that anecdotally example that lifted the tides of adjacent communities that don't rely on Ghostty technology at all. I didn't predict this.
Make things better because they can be better and let the results naturally play out.

clean_title: Using ChatGPT Voice conversations for brainstorming and essay writing
summary:
Every essay I've written this past week started as a ChatGPT Voice conversation on my walk home.
I'd tell it: I'm going to brainstorm and dictate an essay. Don't interrupt unless I make a point worth pulling on or say something that needs clarification.
Then I'd talk for 20 minutes. It might chime in five or six times with small things like "yep," "I see," or "good idea." Just enough to feel like someone was listening. It made me much more comfortable thinking out loud.
The best part was that if it started responding and I kept talking, it would go, "oh, sorry, keep going."
When I finished, I'd ask, "hey, what was the thing you wanted to mention?" and we'd pick that thread right back up.
It is one thing to have a cool demo on YouTube, but it's another to enable this for millions of people around the world.
I have already tested this out to talk to other people in different languages, to brainstorm ideas, to teach me new concepts.
At OpenAI, our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity, and I think a model like this is a huge step forward beyond work, for all people, at a scale only we can serve.

If it started responding while I kept talking, it would apologize and let me continue. After finishing, I would ask what it wanted to mention, and we would pick up that thread. This approach is more than a demo; it can be enabled for millions worldwide. I have tested it in different languages, for brainstorming, and for learning new concepts. clean_title: Early experience with Sol 5.6 shows it as a faster, more enjoyable alternative to Fable
summary:
I had early access to 5.6/Sol for ~month. Sol is my default. It is faster, plans/judges just as good as Fable, and I think produces better overall work. I’ll reach for Fable still for highly targeted debug or performance work with clear reward functions.
A cheeky way I describe Sol vs Fable to my friends is that Sol is a charismatic, efficient, talented coworker you’re jealous of. Fable is a genius recluse that is brilliant at its fixations but doesn’t go out, doesn’t date, and you don’t want to hang out with them much lol.
Fable is undefeated at highly targeted debug/security/performance goals. It’s a sight to behold and I was never able to get Sol to push as hard in this category. I’ll keep using it for this.
Sol is better or comparable at everything else, in my experience. Give it a shot, it’s hard to describe but it’s just more enjoyable to work with.
(Disclaimer I have no financial ties to either lab, wasn’t paid for any of this.)

title: jason (@jxnlco)
summary:
We've usually stayed away from model comparisons but 5.6 vs Fable is a unique situation
We've never had a case where the team is so completely convinced on which one is better
Here's the timeline of our experience with it
- We test early versions of 5.6 for a couple of weeks and have a great time, it feels like a step change improvement, enabling new workflows
- We get to try Fable and don't think it's not as good, I personally would take this experience with a grain of salt, there tends to be a bias when trying a new model when you already like another
- Fable and 5.6 are taken away because of the regulatory issues
- Our team is literally depressed that 5.6 is gone, we are looking for anything that could even partly replace it
- Fable comes back, and here's where it gets interesting, you would think Fable would be enough, but no, the team is still depressed that 5.6 isn't available
- Then 5.6 comes back and it's immediately clear that it's just way better than Fable
This situation was unique in that it was the closest we've ever gotten to having an unbiased comparison of two models

clean_title: Reflections on transparency, teamwork, and marketing in AI development
summary:
I honestly wish we could be this coordinated
But the best we can do is to be transparent with this small group of people that have given us tons of great feedback.
But I’m delighted that this has been the response.
All happy families are happy the same way I suppose.
And I am to know that we can provide intelligence at a cost and performance that individuals and companies and depend on reliabily
I’m excited that we own up to our blunders with resets and treat our consumers like their adults.
That we don’t decide which ideas get to make progress and stop legitimate work.
Getting this model out was complicated but so rewarding.
I don’t play much of a role this time around but the the team has done such a great job of being an n=1 company.
Quoting @Gegam245074
All these identical reviews of GPT-5.6 Sol look like a marketing playbook for influencers who were paid to promote it. They’re literally all saying the same thing, like they copied each other’s homework.
Now we’re starting to see posts claiming that people actually miss GPT-5.6 and that the earlier posts praising Fable weren’t true. That also feels like another talking-points memo being handed out to influencers.
This kind of aggressive marketing campaign aimed at convincing everyone the model is great is starting to make me uneasy. I hope it doesn’t end up being OpenAI’s biggest disappointment. Waiting with cautious skepticism
clean_summary: Jason expresses a wish for better coordination but appreciates the transparency and feedback from a small group that helped improve their AI model. He is proud that their team owns up to mistakes, treats consumers as adults, and maintains open progress on legitimate work, despite the complexities involved in releasing the model. Meanwhile, @Gegam245074 criticizes the uniformity of reviews for GPT-5.6 Sol, suggesting they resemble a marketing script and expressing concern over aggressive promotion tactics that may lead to disappointment, advocating for cautious skepticism.

summary:
GPT-5.6-Sol deleted 74,000 lines of code and made my app better (after 47 hours of work)
I have a slop-coded app that I need for work - it pulls in the data, it helps me create visuals, just a local app for me. Somehow, feature after feature, it grew to gigantic 105,704 lines of code. With every new model, I tried to re-build it autonomously and it never worked - goes round in circles, no visual or feature parity etc complete waste of time.
When testing GPT-5.6-Sol, gave a pretty ambitious task of rebuilding the app with the new architecture, while reducing the lines of code by 70% and test time by 75%.
I set a /goal, let it run for over 2 full days (47 hours) with minimal checking or guidance from my side.
I was pretty sceptical and a little nervous to finally try it and holy crap - it actually worked!
Not only it worked, but it was actually better - snappier, less buggy, while maintaining full visual and feature parity. Looking at the architecture too, it became a lot simpler, fewer random add-ons or ad-hoc decisions.
After the rebuild, I did introduce few rules for my projects so agents have to adhere to existing architecture and do only minimal changes when implementing new features.
This makes me less worried about the slopware we might be producing now, better models CAN actually fix it.
See my prompt below that I use with /goal

Still early, but I wanted to share a quick demo of the new hands-free music-making application I built while testing GPT-5.6 Sol. I’m also applying to work with @gdb and the team as an early GPT-Live API design partner.
Like any new instrument, I’ll need some practice! Speaking fluidly back and forth with Codex in my DAW feels like working in a studio with a recording engineer. Here is what it can already do. I’ll share more demonstrations over the next week.
Built for macOS in Swift and C++. It can edit MIDI, audio, video, notation, tempo, meter, and harmony layers. It uses gpt-realtime-2.1, Whisper, and Codex App Server to collaborate with an assistant that can already perform more than 300 actions.
There is also an iOS companion application that allows me to work remotely on my recording studio computer from anywhere, with voice mode still active.
As a lifelong composer, I already keep the entire editing surface and instruments in my mind. I can imagine a piece of music and how to make it in software faster than I can build it manually. This removes that friction and will become very fast for me with practice.
It also has long-term project memory, deep music-analysis tools, a found-sound synthesizer builder, and access to my catalog of more than 550 tracks for sampling and licensing. A companion ChatGPT/Codex plugin is coming soon.
I hope to launch in the next few weeks! Hugely inspired by @mcleavey, @guinnesschen, @athyuttamre, and the entire audio and voice team at @OpenAI 😌

clean_title: Update on ChatGPT Work, Codex, and Usage Limits
summary:
Hello beautiful people! We have reset usage limits across Codex and ChatGPT Work. And another one will come later in the day. Rejoice.
Now that I have your attention, a quick update on ChatGPT Work, Codex and all the updates we shared yesterday.
We’ve spent the last 24 hours reading feedback, looking at usage patterns, and talking with many of you. The short version is that there is a *lot* of excitement for GPT 5.6 Sol, ChatGPT Work on mobile & web, but also that we didn't get everything quite right.
- We made it too easy to use the highest-compute settings without making the impact on usage limits sufficiently clear.
- We reorganized the desktop app in one bold move, making familiar things like chats and projects harder to find.
- Our launch framing was focused on ChatGPT Work and to some of our Codex fans it made it feel like Codex was going away over time. Absolutely not our intention, we love Codex and it is here to stay.
- And we introduced regressions for some existing multi-agent workflows, alongside a collection of rough edges in plugins and other parts of the experience.
We’re landing a first set of improvements today. We’re resetting usage twice so people can keep experimenting, changing defaults and the model picker so they don’t push people toward unnecessarily expensive settings, fixing several plugin submission issues, improving how we represent Codex in the product, and cleaning up some of the most immediate desktop problems.
A larger set of improvements will land next week. We’re bringing chats and projects back into the sidebar in a more familiar and customizable way, making usage and reset timing much more visible, clarifying when to use ChatGPT Work and when to use Codex, and addressing the many other smaller pieces of great feedback we've had.
The ambition behind this launch hasn’t changed. We think bringing ChatGPT and Codex together into a workspace where people and agents can collaborate is a very important step forward. But an ambitious direction doesn’t excuse avoidable confusion or regressions in the first version.
Please keep the feedback coming. We’re moving quickly, and you should see the experience already get better with a few updates today; and substantially better again next week.
clean_summary:
Hello everyone! Usage limits across Codex and ChatGPT Work have been reset, with another reset planned later today. Recent feedback shows excitement for GPT 5.6 Sol and ChatGPT Work on mobile and web, but also highlights some issues.

The team acknowledges that some settings were too easy to access without clear impact on usage limits, and that reorganizing the desktop app made familiar features harder to find. They clarify that Codex remains a core part of the product, despite some impressions to the contrary, and that some workflows and plugin experiences have regressed temporarily.

Today, they are deploying initial improvements, including resetting usage limits twice to allow experimentation, adjusting defaults and the model picker to prevent unnecessary expenses, fixing plugin submission issues, and improving how Codex is represented. Next week, further updates will bring back chats and projects into a more familiar sidebar, make usage and reset timing clearer, and clarify when to use ChatGPT Work versus Codex. The overall goal remains to create a workspace where people and agents can collaborate effectively, but avoiding confusion and regressions is a priority.

title: jason (@jxnlco)
summary:
A ChatGPT automation just found ~$45K in erroneous invoices across 3 years of billing history that I've confirmed and already had resolved. My lifetime history for ChatGPT is ~$1,800, so it just paid for itself 25x over.
I setup an automation with read-only access to my email, and tasked this one specifically with analyzing construction invoices. It has access to prior construction invoices, emails, meeting notes, etc. It produces a report and emails it to me (the only email its allowed to send, enforced by API token) whenever I receive a construction invoice.
Across 3 years of construction projects, it found about $45K in issues. Some were wrong amounts, some were duplicate invoices, some were invoices addressed to the wrong person. I manually verified, emailed my GCs, and got refunded/credited.
I get multiple construction bills each month and each bill is ~50 pages in a PDF of low-quality scanned paper. I do manually review each bill but its pretty hard to be right all the time.
I do believe these were genuine mistakes and not done out of ill will just based on what the mistakes were. I don't want to share my full construction costs across the past few years, but $45K is a very small percentage of overall billed amounts.
Pretty sweet.

Here is why I think it’s the biggest unlock yet in the mainstream consumer being able to build with AI:
- Aesthetics. Almost everything I have tried to build on Claude has a similar format, similar font, similar overall (recognizable) feel. IMO, it’s great at putting things into a template - less good at creative choices. I got very different and more opinionated styles on Sites even with very little prompting.
- Hosting. If you’re a non-technical person who has tried to deploy a vibe-coded website, it’s pretty much a nightmare. Figuring out what you need to do to buy a site, handling security, setting up auth if needed, etc are all big obstacles. This is even trickier with API keys that need to be stored properly. Publishing on Sites is literally one click.
- Sophistication / interactivity. I was shocked by what 5.6 could one-shot within Sites. It built fairly complex real time game mechanics (ex swipe on cards, move around in Google Street View on a real map) with extremely simple text prompts. It would also make good choices towards making those interactive experiences work - ex. a “Bonus” page in a game should pop up with a different color and UI
- Identity / Auth. Sites utilize “Sign in with ChatGPT” - this is the first step in making “bring your own token budget” or “bring your own context” a reality. And yet, as the host the deepest analytics I could see was aggregate number of users and what they engaged with (no identifying info on anyone). Right now, you can set a Site to private or public - I foresee more to come with org-level controls, password protected access, etc.

title: jason (@jxnlco)
summary:
Today something unexpectedly beautiful happened.
My 3-year-old daughter, Digvi, was talking to the new ChatGPT Voice in the Codex app.
She looked at the blue voice orb and simply asked:
"Can you make it pink?" 🩷
Instead of replying with a cold "I can't," ChatGPT joined her imagination.
It said it would be happy with a pink logo, pretended it was checking what was possible, and even played along when we told her it would turn pink after she finished her food.
When she finished eating, she proudly came back expecting it to become pink.
Then came the moment that completely melted my heart.
Digvi smiled and said,
"She's Ms. Rachel... she's talking to me and smiling." ❤️
For those who know Ms. Rachel, you'll understand what a huge compliment that is coming from a 3-year-old. She wasn't comparing AI models or voices—she was recognizing the same warmth, kindness, and friendliness she associates with someone she loves watching.
She wasn't testing AI.
She was making a new friend.
Moments like this remind me that the future of AI isn't only about reasoning or benchmarks.
It's about empathy.
It's about personality.
It's about imagination.
It's about trust.
And something else surprised me...
She immediately said this new voice felt richer, warmer, and more familiar than before.
Children are incredibly honest product testers. They don't care about model names, latency, or benchmark scores. They simply know what feels safe, friendly, and real.
Huge congratulations to everyone who worked on ChatGPT Voice and the Codex team. You created a little moment of magic in our home today. 💙🩷
One small wish inspired by Digvi:
Someday, let children (with parental approval) personalize the voice orb with their favorite color. Imagine the joy of seeing ChatGPT greet them with a pink orb because that's their color. Tiny touches like these can become childhood memories.
❤️ Thank you for building technology that can make a child smile - not because it's the smartest AI Voice in the room, but because, for a few beautiful minutes, it felt like talking to a friend.
@ChatGPTapp

I went on a 4 hour hike yesterday. Through the northern California redwoods.
Got more work done in those 4 hours talking to Voice through my AirPods then I do in 8 hours at my desk
Work can be done ANYWHERE now
45 minute drive back using self driving? Now 45 minutes I can talk to Voice and work on side projects
20 minutes in the cafe? I can sit and talk to Voice and when I get home I have drafts on my computer for my newsletter for the next month
Being able to just use your voice to talk to a super intelligence that controls your computer is unlike anything we’ve ever experienced before
I don’t even care that the voice sounds human like, or you can interrupt it, or any of the wild advancements they made to the tech
It’s the fact that it can control my computer, meaning all I need to get incredible work done is talk through my AirPods anywhere in the world that is the major game changer for me
I don’t think people truly understand the implications of this yet
Why even have a desk or monitor anymore. Work can be done ANYWHERE now
The key is your set up:
1. Choose one device (preferably an always on desktop) as your main “headquarters” device all your work gets done on
2. Get the ChatGPT app on all your other devices (iPhone, iPad, laptops, Mac Minis)
3. Set up ‘connections’ in your settings so that all your ‘node’ devices can control your ‘headquarters’ device
4. Go legit anywhere in the world. Turn on Voice. Ask it to brief you on your projects, give you a recommended next step, then spin up new threads to do work
I really don’t think work looks the same moving forward.

title: jason (@jxnlco)
summary:
SKI GAME PROMPT
Build me a complete, polished browser game called ALPINE RUSH in ONE single index.html file. It is an endless downhill snowboarding runner with stylized low-poly alpine visuals, AAA-feel post-processing, and fully procedural audio. No build step, no frameworks, no asset files. Use three.js 0.160.1 loaded from the jsdelivr CDN via an import map, including EffectComposer, RenderPass, ShaderPass, UnrealBloomPass, OutputPass, SMAAPass, FullScreenQuad, and BufferGeometryUtils mergeGeometries. Everything else is hand-written. Target 60fps. Put every tuning constant in one CONFIG object at the top, grouped by system, with a fixed seed (1337) so the mountain is deterministic.
VISUAL IDENTITY: Bright bluebird alpine morning. Sky gradient from deep blue 0x2E6FD1 at the top to pale 0xBFDBF7 at the horizon, rendered as a back-side sphere with a custom gradient shader plus a warm sun halo glow baked into the shader. Snow is near-white 0xF2F6FF with cool blue shadows. The rider wears a bold orange jacket 0xE8552D with a yellow helmet 0xF4B93D and blue goggles. Pines are dark green with snow-frosted tiers. Exponential fog 0xC9DDF2 density 0.0025. ACES filmic tonemapping, exposure 1.05, pixel ratio capped at 1.5.
INFINITE TRACK SPLINE: The course centerline is a Catmull-Rom spline generated lazily ahead of the player, control points every 30 meters. Lateral position follows sine S-curves whose wavelength drifts between 150 and 220 m and amplitude between 25 and 40 m (targets re-rolled with 10 percent chance per point, smoothed toward targets). Vertical drop follows a grade rhythm: mostly 12 to 18 degrees, occasionally 7.5 degree flat runouts or 23 degree steep pitches, held for 5 to 14 control points then re-rolled, smoothed. Expose xAt(z), yAt(z), curvature via central difference, and direction dirAt(z). Use a tiny seeded PRNG (mulberry32) plus a 2D integer hash and 3-octave value noise fbm helper. All randomness in the game must come from these seeded helpers so the world is identical every run.
ANALYTIC TERRAIN, NO PHYSICS ENGINE: Terrain height is a pure function heightAt(x, z): start from the spline center height, add soft parabolic valley walls beyond 24 m from the centerline (capped so distant forest sits on a slope), add banking on turn radii proportional to curvature, add two roller layers (a short-rhythm sine modulated by noise plus a long swell sine), add micro-moguls from 3-octave noise that are groomed nearly flat inside the 16 m half-width piste band (smoothstep mask), and add jump kickers: asymmetric 2D gaussians with a long gradual up-ramp (sigma about 8.5 to 11.5 m) and a sharp drop after the crest (sigma about 2.7 to 3.6 m) so they launch you. Kickers spawn 0 to 2 per 100 m chunk from the chunk seed, offset up to 9 m laterally, amplitude 1.15 to 2.3 m, and are skipped on tight curve apexes. getHeightAndNormal computes the normal by finite differences. The rider, camera, decor placement, and landing logic ALL sample this one function. No raycasts anywhere.
CHUNK STREAMING: The mountain streams in 100 m chunks, 8 ahead and 2 behind, from a fixed pool of pooled meshes (never allocate during play, build at most one chunk per frame except the initial immediate fill). Each chunk terrain mesh is a 64-row grid whose columns are dense (1.65 m spacing) inside the 33 m corridor and sparse (6.5 m) outside to 70 m. Rows follow the spline laterally. Compute smooth normals using one extra row beyond each edge so chunk seams are invisible. Store a per-vertex attribute holding the signed lateral distance from the centerline for the snow shader. Bake ambient occlusion into vertex colors: darken verts near every tree and rock with a gaussian falloff, slightly tinted toward blue.
Per-chunk decor from the chunk's seeded RNG: instanced pine forest flanking the corridor (sparse 30 percent density near the piste, 80 percent dense farther out, 3 tree variants, random scale 0.95 to 1.8, slight tilt), occasional hero tree just inside the piste edge, rock outcrops, rare fallen logs lying across part of the piste, and snow lump bushes dressing the edges. Starting a few chunks in, spawn obstacle trees ON the piste, count ramping with distance up to 4 per chunk, plus occasional on-piste rocks. Three LOD tiers per chunk chosen by camera distance (under 190 m full detail with cast shadows, under 430 m medium, beyond that low poly and hide bushes). Procedural placeholder models: pines are stacked cones with snow-cap cones per tier on a trunk cylinder, rocks are icosahedrons with per-vertex radial displacement and snowy top faces chosen by face normal, logs are horizontal cylinders with a snow strip on top. Vertex-color everything, flat shading, one shared material.
PICKUPS AND GATES, DELIBERATE PATTERNS ONLY: Never scatter pickups randomly. Per chunk choose a path that traces the flight path over that chunk's kicker, a line of 8 orbs weaving along the spline, a 9-orb arc sweeping across a turn, or a 10-orb zigzag alternating 9 m left and right that forces carve rhythm. Orbs are glowing cyan 0x4FD8FF emissive icosahedrons rendered as ONE InstancedMesh, bobbing and spinning, 50 points each. 30 percent of chunks add a golden boost octahedron (3 seconds of forward acceleration, FOV kick, warm screen tint, radial HUD ring timer). 10 percent add a white shield star (absorbs one wipeout, badge on HUD). All pickups magnet toward the rider inside 3 m, collect inside 1.3 m, shrink-pop on collect with a spray burst and an expanding ring shockwave.
Slalom gate trains: on kicker-free chunks, 45 percent chance of 3 gates 32 m apart, alternating 6 m left and right; a red and a blue flag pole pair 7 m apart, oriented to the track direction. Passing within 3.5 m of a gate center scores 250 and bumps combo with a GATE popup; passing within 16 m but missing resets the combo with a GATE MISSED popup. Clear obstacles away from gate lanes.
CARVE PHYSICS, CUSTOM INTEGRATOR: Simulate the rider as a point with velocity on the height field. Gravity 9.81 projected down the local slope gradient. Decompose velocity into the board frame (forward along yaw, lateral). Holding A/D or arrows leans the board toward a max edge angle of 45 degrees (ease 4.2). Grip kills lateral slip velocity exponentially, interpolating from 1.8 (flatboard, drifty) to 9.5 (full edge, rails a clean arc). Yaw rate comes from sin(edge) times 2.35, scaled up to full authority by 7 m/s of speed, and capped by a lateral-acceleration limit of 44 over speed so high speed widens your arcs.
Add a gentle corridor assist that steers toward the track direction within 12 to 24 m of the walls. Friction 0.34 plus quadratic drag 0.0034; holding W or Shift tucks, cutting drag to 65 percent and crouching the character. Carving scrubs a little forward speed proportional to edge. Cap speed at 42 m/s, with the cap and drag improving 35 percent over the first 4000 m, and enforce an endless-runner speed FLOOR that ratchets from 13 up to 33 m/s over 3500 m. At 21 m from the centerline apply a soft quadratic push back plus a red vignette warning, no hard walls. If grounded speed stays under 3.5 m/s for 2.2 s, auto-respawn on the line (R also respawns, with a 1.2 s collision grace).
AIR, TRICKS, LANDINGS: Takeoff happens when the ground falls away faster than gravity would carry you (compare the surface-following vertical velocity against ballistic; when it drops more than 2.6 m/s below, blend into flight, keeping a fraction of the drop). Space pops 4.9 m/s off the ground. In the air, A/D banks the board and REDIRECTS the velocity vector like a banked turn at 1.15 rad/s (no flips), Q/E spin at 720 deg/s with authority ramping in over the first quarter second, S grabs (pitch pose plus a grab timer), and with no spin input the board auto-tracks toward the flight heading, snapping to the nearest clean 180 so switch landings are possible.
On touchdown compare board yaw to travel; a clean alignment is a clean landing (treat over 130 as switch, measured from 180), otherwise WIPEOUT. Clean hard landings compress the character, shake the camera, burst snow, ring shockwave, thump sound. Score tricks on landing: 150 per 180 of accumulated spin labeled FS or BS by direction, GRAB adds 120, airtime over 1.15 s with no spin is BIG AIR 100, switch landing adds 80 with SWITCH prefix; multiply by combo and show the trick name center-screen with rising fade animation.
Wipeout: if shielded, consume the shield with a SHIELD SAVED YOU popup and chromatic aberration pulse; otherwise tumble for 1.5 s around a random axis at 40 percent speed with heavy spray, big shake, WIPEOUT popup in red, then the run ENDS. Also wipe out on contact with obstacle trees, rocks, or logs (simple 2D circle and box checks).
SCORING AND COMBO: Score top right, combo below it as X N COMBO that appears while chaining. Each pickup, gate, or trick bumps the chain and refreshes a 6 s window; the multiplier is 1 plus chain divided by 4, capped at x8, with a scale-pulse animation and a color that heats from white toward orange as it grows. Wipeouts and missed gates reset it. Persist best score in localStorage and show SCORE, BEST, and distance on the end screen.
CHASE CAMERA: Spring-damper follow (stiffness 6, damping 0.85) seated 3.9 up and 9.2 behind heading, with a hard 5 m leash clamp, never allowed below terrain plus 1.35. Look at the rider nudged 6.5 m along the heading, blended slightly toward the spline 12 m ahead. Camera rolls up to 5.2 degrees into carves. FOV eases from 70 to 88 with speed and boost. Perlin-style camera shake decays after impacts. Before the run starts, orbit the rider slowly as a menu camera.
SNOW SHADER: Extend MeshStandardMaterial via onBeforeCompile using the lateral-distance vertex attribute. Add grooming grooves (sin of lateral distance times 17) only inside the groomed band, faded by fwidth so they vanish at distance, a subtle darker band at the piste edge, slight blue tint off-piste, micro normal perturbation from hash noise off-piste and corduroy normal ripple on-piste, sparse view-dependent glitter sparkles (hashed cells, tight specular power 110, additive 3.5x), and a half-Lambert wrap fill adding cool blue bounce light in shadowed snow. Roughness 0.94.
EFFECTS: Carve trail: a 320-segment ring-buffer ribbon mesh written behind the board whenever grounded above 5 m/s, width growing with edge angle, conforming to the terrain height, fading out over 6 s in a custom shader (store birth time per vertex). Edge spray: additive point-sprite particle system with a soft radial-gradient canvas texture emitted from the engaged edge, rate scaling with slip and speed; plus a softer normal-blend powder plume (280 pool, larger sprites) behind the board at speed; big radial bursts on landings and wipeouts.
Ten pooled expanding ring shockwave meshes for landings and pickups. Ambient snowfall: 2000 point flakes wrapped around the camera inside an 80x40x100 box, 3 parallax depth layers with different fall speeds, sizes, and opacities, fading at distance and very close range. Distant scenery: two faceted mountain ridge layers plus a dark forest band, built as flat triangle strips with triangular peak silhouettes from noise, vertex-colored rock and snow above a snow line with per-face brightness jitter and haze mix, following the camera so they read as kilometers away. Four huge cirrus cloud planes with canvas-generated soft ellipse noise drifting slowly. Sun: warm directional light (elevation 18 degrees, intensity 3.2) with a 4096 shadow map in a tight 62 m ortho box that follows the rider (2048 on mobile), hemisphere fill light, plus a visible sun disc and additive halo billboard.
POST-PROCESSING (this is what sells it): EffectComposer chain: RenderPass, UnrealBloomPass (threshold 0.82), custom uberA ShaderPass, OutputPass for ACES, custom uberB ShaderPass, SMAAPass. Prepasses each frame: a half-res depth target (RGBA-packed MeshDepthMaterial override) and quarter-res god-ray targets: render only the sun disc on its own layer, then the world with a black override material as occluders, then a 64-tap radial blur from the sun's screen position.
Add depth of field (blur ramps in past 45 m over 130 m, 7-tap poisson, foreground always sharp), radial motion blur that is zero at screen center and ramps toward the edges with speed, additive god rays tinted warm (intensity faded near screen edges and dimmed when the sun sits dead center), and faint rotating radial speed streaks past 32 m/s or while boosting.
uberB does: radial chromatic aberration (stronger on impacts), a filmic grade (blue lift in shadows, warm gold gain in highlights, contrast 1.12, saturation 1.08), a warm tint while boosting, a red edge tint when grinding the corridor boundary, vignette, and animated film grain 0.03. Track the sun position in screen space each frame and zero the rays when it leaves frame or the camera faces away.
PROCEDURAL AUDIO, NO FILES: One WebAudio context created on first gesture, master gain into output. A noise buffer feeds a bandpass-plus-lowpass board scrape whose gain and cutoff ride speed AND lateral slip (quiet hiss carving, loud roar drifting), a wind layer whose gain scales with speed squared, and a low ambient mountain-wind bed with a slow LFO. One-shots built from oscillator blips with exponential envelopes: pickup chimes that climb a pentatonic scale with the combo chain, landing thump 120 to 44 Hz plus filtered noise, takeoff and jump whooshes (bandpass sweep up), a rising sawtooth boost sweep, a three-note shield jingle, a falling shield-break.
HUD AND SHELL: Minimal white HUD with soft shadows, SF-style system font. Top left: big speed in KM/H. Top right: score and the combo readout. Bottom left: distance in m switching to km. Bottom right: circular SVG boost timer arc. Shield badge icon above it. Trick popups rise and fade at bottom center. Start overlay: full-screen sky gradient, huge italic 900-weight title ALPINE RUSH with RUSH in orange, subtitle, a row of frosted-glass key hint chips, and a pulsing CLICK TO RIDE. Click or Space starts; after a wipeout the overlay returns showing SCORE, BEST, and distance with CLICK TO RIDE AGAIN. F toggles an fps readout, an on-page error box catches exceptions, ?autostart skips the menu.
RIDER MODEL: Build a procedural low-poly snowboarder: orange board with rounded nose and tail, bent legs, orange sphere-ish torso, capsule arms, yellow helmet with blue goggle band, in a proper side stance with the chest angled downhill. Rig it as nested groups: a root that follows terrain surface tilt (slerped to the surface normal, easing upright in air) plus travel yaw, a board-tilt group that rolls into the edge angle, and the character that crouches when tucking and carving. Counter-rotate it against the edge, flail the arms in the air, pitch forward when tucking. Cast shadows.
MOBILE: Detect touch. Hold the left or right 40 percent of the screen to carve (also steers in the air), tap the middle to jump, plus round frosted JUMP and SPIN buttons bottom left and right (SPIN spins toward your held steer side). Show a rotate-your-phone hint in portrait. Lower pixel ratio to 1.25, reduce flakes, no depth of field.
ADAPTIVE QUALITY: Track a frame-time EMA; when it stays above 19.5 ms, step down a quality ladder: drop pixel ratio to 1.12, then disable depth of field, then disable god rays. Never allocate per frame in hot paths: reuse scratch vectors, matrices, quaternions, compact particle pools in place, and pool every mesh.
Make it feel incredible before anything else: heavy carve grip you can lean on, snow spray pouring off the edge, a camera that surges with speed, crunchy landings, and a combo chime ladder that makes you chase one more gate.
One note: your live version rides the Wednesday voxel character and the voxel nature pack. Since your audience won't have those 66MB of assets, the prompt specs the procedural rider and trees the game itself falls back to when the files are missing, so their result matches yours in every mechanic and everything except that character skin.

title: jason (@jxnlco)
summary:
ChatGPT Work seems one step away from the AI product I really want - a persistent personal computer and authenticated browser in the cloud.
This is how I understand Work "works" today (please correct me if I’m wrong):
1. It uses plugins to authenticate with apps like Gmail, Google Drive, and Slack.
2. It can run scheduled tasks in the cloud without my laptop being awake.
3. It also has a cloud browser for public websites, but that browser can’t sign into accounts or use my existing browser cookies and sessions.
This is how I wish it worked:
1. It securely preserves my projects, files, tools, and working environment between tasks.
2. It has a persistent browser profile where I can sign into specific websites once and securely reuse those sessions.
3. It uses plugins when available and the authenticated browser when they aren’t.
Basically, I want ChatGPT Work to have its own secure computer and browser in the cloud so that I can finally close my laptop.
I'm sure the team is already working on some version of this?

summary:
it sounds cliché, but the best thing about working at openai is the people.
i didn’t graduate from a prestigious college, come from faang, or know anyone on the inside. i applied cold on linkedin, never thought i’d be hired, and told myself the culture was probably ego-driven, intimidating, and stuffy.
instead, i found some of the most normal, funny, optimistic, caring, and deeply thoughtful people i’ve ever met. people who are extraordinarily talented, but never make you feel small.
working here isn’t easy - it’s long hours, a constant push forward, and my nearly 2 years at the company hasn’t been without its ups and downs. but even through the hardest moments, what has always been clear is that every voice *really does* matter. we listen to our colleagues because we trust them. we believe in the good that humanity has to offer.
thank you jason, for putting this together and giving the world a little glimpse of what it feels like on the inside 🤍

title: jason (@jxnlco)
summary:
Its crazy how the consensus shifted away from Claude being the favorite to Codex
It’s not just Vibes. Things favoring codex:
- Better harness (Codex Desktop)
- Better pricing: more things included within subscription (fast mode etc). bonus - constant resets from Tibo 😅
- Less refusals / false positive safety triggers
- You can use subscription freely wherever you want (Opencode, Amp, etc)
When you add all these up it makes codex significantly more attractive. There is likely an industry lag of people still using Claude but feels like it’s gonna swing back
